claim: HCC is the fifth most frequently diagnosed cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide.
source: HCC is the fifth most frequently diagnosed cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide (Villanueva, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Villanueva, 2019

claim: The molecular landscape of HCC is very complex and includes multiple genetic and epigenetic modifications.
source: The molecular landscape of HCC is very complex and includes multiple genetic and epigenetic modifications that could represent new diagnosis and therapeutic targets.

claim: Hoshida et al. classified HCC into S1, S2, and S3 subtypes by means of their histological, pathological, and molecular signatures.
source: For instance, Hoshida et al. classified HCC into S1, S2, and S3 subtypes by means of their histological, pathological, and molecular signatures (Hoshida et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoshida et al., 2009

claim: S1 tumors exhibit high TGF-β and Wnt signaling activity but do not harbor mutations or genomic changes.
source: S1 tumors exhibit high TGF-β and Wnt signaling activity but do not harbor mutations or genomic changes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoshida et al., 2009 in the preceding sentence

claim: S1 tumors are relatively large, poorly differentiated, and associated with poor survival.
source: The tumors are relatively large, poorly differentiated, and associated with poor survival.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoshida et al., 2009 in the preceding context

claim: S2 tumors have increased levels of Myc and phospho-Akt and overexpress α-fetoprotein.
source: S2 tumors have increased levels of Myc and phospho-Akt and overexpress α-fetoprotein, an HCC serum biomarker.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoshida et al., 2009 in the preceding context

claim: α-fetoprotein is an HCC serum biomarker.
source: S2 tumors have increased levels of Myc and phospho-Akt and overexpress α-fetoprotein, an HCC serum biomarker.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in the field

claim: S3 tumors harbor mutations in CTNNB1 (β-catenin) but tend to be well-differentiated and are associated with good overall survival.
source: S3 tumors harbor mutations in CTNNB1 (β-catenin) but tend to be well-differentiated and are associated with good overall survival.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoshida et al., 2009 in the preceding context

claim: Sorafenib is a multi-kinase inhibitor that targets Raf, receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), and the platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR).
source: The standard of care for advanced HCC is treatment with sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor that targets Raf, receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), and the platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations in the following sentence

claim: Sorafenib extends the median survival time from 7.9 months to 10.7 months.
source: Sorafenib extends the median survival time from 7.9 months to 10.7 months, and lenvatinib, a multiple VEGFR kinase inhibitor, has been reported to extend survival to 13.6 months (Llovet et al., 2018; Philip et al., 2005; Rimassa and Santoro, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Llovet et al., 2018; Philip et al., 2005; Rimassa and Santoro, 2009

claim: Lenvatinib, a multiple VEGFR kinase inhibitor, has been reported to extend survival to 13.6 months.
source: Sorafenib extends the median survival time from 7.9 months to 10.7 months, and lenvatinib, a multiple VEGFR kinase inhibitor, has been reported to extend survival to 13.6 months (Llovet et al., 2018; Philip et al., 2005; Rimassa and Santoro, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Llovet et al., 2018; Philip et al., 2005; Rimassa and Santoro, 2009

claim: The global death toll per year from HCC reaches 700,000.
source: However, even with the most advanced forms of treatment, the global death toll per year reaches 700,000, creating a mortality ratio of 1.07 with a 5-year survival rate of 18% (Ferlay et al., 2010; Siegel et al., 2014; Villanueva, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferlay et al., 2010; Siegel et al., 2014; Villanueva, 2019

claim: HCC has a mortality ratio of 1.07 with a 5-year survival rate of 18%.
source: However, even with the most advanced forms of treatment, the global death toll per year reaches 700,000, creating a mortality ratio of 1.07 with a 5-year survival rate of 18% (Ferlay et al., 2010; Siegel et al., 2014; Villanueva, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferlay et al., 2010; Siegel et al., 2014; Villanueva, 2019

claim: The ENCODE consortium revealed that as much as 80% of the human genome can be transcribed, while only 2% of the genome encodes for proteins.
source: The ENCODE consortium revealed that as much as 80% of the human genome can be transcribed, while only 2% of the genome encodes for proteins (Djebali et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Djebali et al., 2012

claim: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are transcripts from 200 nucleotides (nt) to over 100 kilobases (kb) in length.
source: Thousands of transcripts from 200 nucleotides (nt) to over 100 kilobases (kb) in length, called long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), are the largest and most diverse class of non-protein-coding transcripts.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in the field

claim: lncRNAs are the largest and most diverse class of non-protein-coding transcripts.
source: Thousands of transcripts from 200 nucleotides (nt) to over 100 kilobases (kb) in length, called long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), are the largest and most diverse class of non-protein-coding transcripts.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in the field

claim: lncRNAs commonly originate from intergenic regions or introns and can be transcribed in the sense or antisense direction.
source: They commonly originate from intergenic regions or introns and can be transcribed in the sense or antisense direction.
evidence: Supported by review citation in the following sentence (Rinn and Chang, 2012)

claim: Most lncRNAs are produced by RNA polymerase II and can be capped, spliced, and poly-adenylated.
source: Most are produced by RNA polymerase II and can be capped, spliced, and poly-adenylated (reviewed in Rinn and Chang, 2012).
evidence: Supported by review citation to Rinn and Chang, 2012

claim: Many lncRNAs are expressed in a cell- or tissue-specific manner.
source: Strikingly, many are expressed in a cell- or tissue-specific manner and undergo changes in expression level during cellular differentiation and in cancers (Costa, 2005; Dinger et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costa, 2005; Dinger et al., 2008

claim: lncRNAs undergo changes in expression level during cellular differentiation and in cancers.
source: Strikingly, many are expressed in a cell- or tissue-specific manner and undergo changes in expression level during cellular differentiation and in cancers (Costa, 2005; Dinger et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costa, 2005; Dinger et al., 2008

claim: Some lncRNAs are dysregulated in HCC and have the potential to be specific to a subtype of HCC.
source: These lncRNAs present as an exciting class of regulatory molecules to pursue as some are dysregulated in HCC and have the potential to be specific to a subtype of HCC (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2015

claim: HOTAIR acts in trans by recruiting the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), the lysine-specific histone demethylase (LSD1), and the CoREST/REST H3K4 demethylase complex to their target genes.
source: This transcript acts in trans by recruiting the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), the lysine-specific histone demethylase (LSD1), and the CoREST/REST H3K4 demethylase complex to their target genes (Ezponda and Licht, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ezponda and Licht, 2014

claim: HOTAIR promotes HCC cell migration and invasion by repressing RNA binding motif protein 38 (RBM38).
source: HOTAIR promotes HCC cell migration and invasion by repressing RNA binding motif protein 38 (RBM38), which is otherwise targeted by p53 to induce cell cycle arrest in G1 (Shu et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shu et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2015

claim: RBM38 is targeted by p53 to induce cell cycle arrest in G1.
source: HOTAIR promotes HCC cell migration and invasion by repressing RNA binding motif protein 38 (RBM38), which is otherwise targeted by p53 to induce cell cycle arrest in G1 (Shu et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shu et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2015

claim: lncRNAs can function through inhibitory sequestration of miRNAs and transcription factors.
source: Another mechanism through which lncRNAs function involves inhibitory sequestration of miRNAs and transcription factors (Cesana et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cesana et al., 2011

claim: The lncRNA HULC sequesters miR-372, which represses the protein kinase PRKACB, and downregulates the tumor suppressor gene CDKN2C (p18).
source: In HCC, the lncRNA HULC (highly upregulated in liver cancer) sequesters miR-372, which represses the protein kinase PRKACB, and downregulates the tumor suppressor gene CDKN2C (p18) (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2010

claim: MALAT1 is a highly conserved lncRNA that controls expression of a set of genes associated with cell proliferation and migration.
source: Similarly, the highly conserved MALAT1 lncRNA controls expression of a set of genes associated with cell proliferation and migration and is upregulated in many solid carcinomas (Amodio et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Amodio et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2007

claim: MALAT1 is upregulated in many solid carcinomas.
source: Similarly, the highly conserved MALAT1 lncRNA controls expression of a set of genes associated with cell proliferation and migration and is upregulated in many solid carcinomas (Amodio et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Amodio et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2007

claim: siRNA knockdown of MALAT1 in HCC cell lines decreases cell proliferation, migration, and invasion.
source: siRNA knockdown of MALAT1 in HCC cell lines decreases cell proliferation, migration, and invasion (Lai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lai et al., 2012

claim: The authors reanalyzed naïve and differentiated transcriptomes of mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) in the context of the GENCODE M20 annotation.
source: Here, we reanalyzed naïve and differentiated transcriptomes of mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) in the context of the GENCODE M20 annotation.
evidence: Supported by description of methods in the manuscript

claim: The authors identified a lncRNA, Gm19705, that is overexpressed in hepatocellular carcinoma and mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: We identified a long non-coding RNA, Gm19705, that is overexpressed in hepatocellular carcinoma and mouse embryonic stem cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The authors named the lncRNA Gm19705 as PHAROH (Pluripotency and Hepatocyte Associated RNA Overexpressed in HCC).
source: We named this RNA Pluripotency and Hepatocyte Associated RNA Overexpressed in HCC, or PHAROH.
evidence: Explicit statement in the abstract

claim: Depletion of PHAROH impacts cell proliferation and migration.
source: Depletion of PHAROH impacts cell proliferation and migration, which can be rescued by ectopic expression of PHAROH.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The impact of PHAROH depletion on cell proliferation and migration can be rescued by ectopic expression of PHAROH.
source: Depletion of PHAROH impacts cell proliferation and migration, which can be rescued by ectopic expression of PHAROH.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: RNA-seq analysis of PHAROH knockouts revealed that a large number of genes with decreased expression contain a Myc motif in their promoter.
source: RNA-seq analysis of PHAROH knockouts revealed that a large number of genes with decreased expression contain a Myc motif in their promoter.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and motif analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: MYC is decreased in PHAROH knockout cells at the protein level, but not the mRNA level.
source: MYC is decreased in knockout cells at the protein level, but not the mRNA level.
evidence: Supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data presented in the manuscript

claim: RNA-antisense pulldown identified nucleolysin TIAR as a protein that binds to a 71-nt hairpin within PHAROH.
source: RNA-antisense pulldown identified nucleolysin TIAR, a translational repressor, to bind to a 71-nt hairpin within PHAROH, sequestration of which increases MYC translation.
evidence: Supported by RAP-MS and RNA EMSA data presented in the manuscript

claim: TIAR is a translational repressor.
source: RNA-antisense pulldown identified nucleolysin TIAR, a translational repressor, to bind to a 71-nt hairpin within PHAROH, sequestration of which increases MYC translation.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript

claim: Sequestration of TIAR by PHAROH increases MYC translation.
source: RNA-antisense pulldown identified nucleolysin TIAR, a translational repressor, to bind to a 71-nt hairpin within PHAROH, sequestration of which increases MYC translation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data including luciferase assays and western blots presented in the manuscript

claim: PHAROH regulates MYC translation by sequestering TIAR.
source: In summary, our data suggest that PHAROH regulates MYC translation by sequestering TIAR and as such represents a potentially exciting diagnostic or therapeutic target in hepatocellular carcinoma.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental data including RAP-MS, RNA EMSA, luciferase assays, and western blots

claim: PHAROH represents a potentially exciting diagnostic or therapeutic target in hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: In summary, our data suggest that PHAROH regulates MYC translation by sequestering TIAR and as such represents a potentially exciting diagnostic or therapeutic target in hepatocellular carcinoma.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing PHAROH's role in HCC cell proliferation and MYC regulation

claim: ESCs and NPCs independently cluster in principal component analysis.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the processed data showed that ESCs and NPCs independently cluster, and the difference between ESC cell lines (AB2.2) and mouse-derived ESCs only accounted for 4% of the variance (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: The difference between ESC cell lines (AB2.2) and mouse-derived ESCs only accounted for 4% of the variance in PCA.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the processed data showed that ESCs and NPCs independently cluster, and the difference between ESC cell lines (AB2.2) and mouse-derived ESCs only accounted for 4% of the variance (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: 147 ESC-specific transcripts were identified with FPKM value >1 and more than twofold upregulation in ESCs compared to NPCs.
source: Additionally, we prioritized transcripts with an FPKM value >1, and those that were more than twofold upregulated in ESCs compared to NPCs. This left us with 147 ESC-specific transcripts.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis described in the manuscript

claim: A final candidate list of 40 lncRNAs that are enriched in ESCs and dysregulated in cancer was identified.
source: A final candidate list of 40 lncRNAs that are enriched in ESCs, and dysregulated in cancer, was identified (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by the filtering workflow and data analysis described in the manuscript

claim: The candidate list contains several previously identified lncRNAs that have been found to be dysregulated in cancer (NEAT1, FIRRE, XIST, DANCR, and GAS5).
source: Our candidate list contains lncRNAs that have a wide range of expression and also contains several previously identified lncRNAs that have been found to be dysregulated in cancer (NEAT1, FIRRE, XIST, DANCR, and GAS5), verifying the validity of the approach (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Ji et al., 2019; Soudyab et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ji et al., 2019; Soudyab et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016

claim: lncRNAs are generally not pan-expressed, but are rather tissue specific.
source: lncRNAs are known to have distinct expression patterns across different tissues, and our results support the notion that lncRNAs are generally not pan-expressed.
evidence: Supported by analysis of ENCODE expression datasets shown in Figure 1C

claim: Many of the identified lncRNAs are enriched in embryonic liver.
source: Interestingly, many of the identified lncRNAs are enriched in embryonic liver, which is the organ with the most regenerative capacity, yet never grows past its original size.
evidence: Supported by analysis of ENCODE expression datasets shown in Figure 1C

claim: LINC00862 was altered in 13% of all HCC patient cases according to TCGA data.
source: Out of these four lncRNAs that were detected to be amplified in HCC, LINC00862 was the highest at 13% of all liver cancer cases (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Levels of LINC00862 were elevated in HCC tumor nodules and cirrhotic liver.
source: We assayed LINC00862 expression in human samples obtained from healthy and cirrhotic livers and HCC nodules. Indeed, we found that levels of LINC00862 were elevated in HCC tumor nodules, but also in cirrhotic liver, suggesting that it may play a role in HCC progression (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D

claim: LINC00862 may play a role in HCC progression.
source: Indeed, we found that levels of LINC00862 were elevated in HCC tumor nodules, but also in cirrhotic liver, suggesting that it may play a role in HCC progression (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on inference from the expression data showing LINC00862 upregulation in cirrhotic liver and HCC

claim: LINC00862 is upregulated in numerous HCC cell lines compared to the normal human liver cell line, THLE-2.
source: In addition, we also assayed LINC00862 expression in human HCC cell lines and found it to be upregulated in numerous HCC cell lines compared to the normal human liver cell line, THLE-2 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E

claim: GM19705 has 51% sequence identity with LINC00862.
source: While much shorter, GM19705 has 51% sequence identity and the gene order is syntenically conserved, although a reversal event most likely occurred within the locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis described in the manuscript

claim: The gene order of GM19705 and LINC00862 is syntenically conserved, although a reversal event most likely occurred within the locus.
source: While much shorter, GM19705 has 51% sequence identity and the gene order is syntenically conserved, although a reversal event most likely occurred within the locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by synteny analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Weighted gene correlation network analysis of GM19705 identified that its expression is highly correlated with those of cell cycle genes, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2.
source: Weighted gene correlation network analysis of GM19705 identified that its expression is highly correlated with those of cell cycle genes, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by WGCNA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: GO term analysis of the cluster containing GM19705 identified cell cycle processes as highly enriched.
source: GO term analysis of the cluster identified cell cycle processes as highly enriched, indicating that GM19705 may play a role in the regulation of the cell cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: GM19705 may play a role in the regulation of the cell cycle.
source: GO term analysis of the cluster identified cell cycle processes as highly enriched, indicating that GM19705 may play a role in the regulation of the cell cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on inference from GO term analysis

claim: GM19705 expression is low overall in normal adult mouse liver, but highly expressed exclusively in a subset of hepatocytes.
source: Reanalysis of previously published single-cell analysis of normal adult mouse liver (Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018) identified GM19705 expression to be low overall, as expected, but highly expressed exclusively in a subset of hepatocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of single-cell data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: PHAROH is an intergenic lncRNA located on mouse chr1:1qE4.
source: PHAROH is an intergenic lncRNA located on mouse chr1:1qE4.
evidence: Supported by genomic location data

claim: 5′ and 3′ RACE revealed the presence of two isoforms of PHAROH that share two common exons and are both ~450 nt.
source: 5′ and 3′ rapid extension of cDNA ends (RACE) revealed the presence of two isoforms that share two common exons and are both ~450 nt (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RACE data shown in Figure 2A

claim: In silico analysis of the coding potential by three independent algorithms (CPAT/CPC and PhyloCSF) all point towards the low coding potential score of PHAROH.
source: In silico analysis of the coding potential by three independent algorithms, which use codon bias (CPAT/CPC) and comparative genomics (PhyloCSF), all point towards the low coding potential score of PHAROH, compared to the Gapdh control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by coding potential analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: PHAROH is seven- to ninefold enriched in E14 and E18 embryonic liver compared to adult liver.
source: We confirmed expression levels of PHAROH in developing liver by assaying the liver bud from E14 and E18 embryos and found that they were seven- to ninefold enriched compared to adult liver (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B

claim: PHAROH expression is exclusive to the liver, and not to hematopoietic cells in the embryo.
source: Because the liver is one of the main sites of hematopoiesis in the embryo, we measured PHAROH levels in embryonic blood and found that expression was exclusive to the liver, and not to hematopoietic cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: PHAROH was found to be upregulated in a partial hepatectomy (PH) model of liver regeneration.
source: PHAROH was also found to be upregulated in a partial hepatectomy (PH) model of liver regeneration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), where the expression was correlated with time points of concerted DNA synthesis, but did not fluctuate across the cell cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: PHAROH expression was correlated with time points of concerted DNA synthesis in the partial hepatectomy model, but did not fluctuate across the cell cycle.
source: PHAROH was also found to be upregulated in a partial hepatectomy (PH) model of liver regeneration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), where the expression was correlated with time points of concerted DNA synthesis, but did not fluctuate across the cell cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E

claim: HCC tumor nodules in the DEN-induced carcinogenic model had elevated levels of PHAROH.
source: To confirm PHAROH's involvement in HCC, we used a diethylnitrosamine (DEN)-induced carcinogenic model of liver injury. By 11 months post DEN treatment, we were able to visualize HCC tumor nodules, which had elevated levels of PHAROH (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C

claim: PHAROH was 3- to 4-fold more enriched in Hepa1-6 and Hepa1c1c7 HCC cell lines than in ESCs.
source: In order to facilitate the molecular and biochemical study of PHAROH, we chose two mouse HCC cell lines, Hepa1-6 and Hepa1c1c7, and indeed found that PHAROH was 3- to 4-fold more enriched than in ESCs, and 8- to 10-fold increased over the AML12 mouse normal hepatocyte cell line (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D

claim: PHAROH was 8- to 10-fold increased in Hepa1-6 and Hepa1c1c7 HCC cell lines over the AML12 mouse normal hepatocyte cell line.
source: In order to facilitate the molecular and biochemical study of PHAROH, we chose two mouse HCC cell lines, Hepa1-6 and Hepa1c1c7, and indeed found that PHAROH was 3- to 4-fold more enriched than in ESCs, and 8- to 10-fold increased over the AML12 mouse normal hepatocyte cell line (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D

claim: PHAROH is entirely nuclear in ESCs, with an average of 3–5 foci per cell.
source: Single-molecule RNA-FISH revealed that PHAROH is entirely nuclear in ESCs, with an average of 3–5 foci per cell, whereas it is evenly distributed between the nucleus and cytoplasm in Hepa1-6 cells, with an average of 25 foci per cell (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-FISH data shown in Figure 2E, F

claim: PHAROH is evenly distributed between the nucleus and cytoplasm in Hepa1-6 cells, with an average of 25 foci per cell.
source: Single-molecule RNA-FISH revealed that PHAROH is entirely nuclear in ESCs, with an average of 3–5 foci per cell, whereas it is evenly distributed between the nucleus and cytoplasm in Hepa1-6 cells, with an average of 25 foci per cell (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-FISH data shown in Figure 2E, F

claim: Isoform 1 of PHAROH is expressed mostly in ESCs while isoform 2 dominates HCC cell lines.
source: Isoform 1 is expressed mostly in ESCs while isoform 2 of PHAROH dominates HCC cell lines (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq tracks and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: Cellular fractionation of Hepa1-6 cells corroborates the RNA-FISH-determined localization of PHAROH.
source: Cellular fractionation of Hepa1-6 cells corroborates the RNA-FISH-determined localization of PHAROH as well, which GAPDH and MALAT1 localized correctly to previously determined cellular fractions (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by cellular fractionation data shown in Figure 2G

claim: PHAROH has a relatively longer half-life in the Hepa1-6 cell line (10.8 hr) compared to MALAT1 (8.0 hr) and XIST (4.2 hr).
source: It was also determined that PHAROH has a relatively longer half-life in the Hepa1-6 cell line (10.8 hr) compared to MALAT1 (8.0 hr) and XIST (4.2 hr) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H; Tani et al., 2012; Yamada et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by α-amanitin treatment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H

claim: All selected PHAROH knockout clones had the correct homozygous deletion when assayed by genomic PCR.
source: 85% of the cells were GFP+/mCherry+, and we selected four clones for subsequent analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). All selected clones had the correct homozygous deletion when assayed by genomic PCR (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by genomic PCR data shown in Figure 3A

claim: qRT-PCR indicated that PHAROH was knocked down 80–95% in the selected clones.
source: qRT-PCR indicated that PHAROH was knocked down 80–95% (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The doubling time of the PHAROH knockout clones increased to 18.2 hr compared to the wildtype doubling time of 14.8 hr.
source: We assayed the proliferative state of the PHAROH knockout clones and found a decrease in proliferation. The doubling time of the knockout clones increased to 18.2 hr compared to the wildtype doubling time of 14.8 hr, and ectopic expression of PHAROH reduced the doubling time to nearly wildtype levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by doubling time data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Ectopic expression of PHAROH reduced the doubling time of knockout clones to nearly wildtype levels.
source: The doubling time of the knockout clones increased to 18.2 hr compared to the wildtype doubling time of 14.8 hr, and ectopic expression of PHAROH reduced the doubling time to nearly wildtype levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by doubling time data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Ectopic expression of PHAROH successfully rescued the proliferation phenotype in the knockout clones, suggesting that PHAROH functions in trans.
source: Ectopic expression of PHAROH also successfully rescued the proliferation phenotype in the knockout clones, suggesting that PHAROH functions in trans (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Migration distance was decreased by 50% in the PHAROH knockout clones.
source: Migration distance was also decreased by 50% in the knockout clones (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 3E

claim: ASOs complementary to PHAROH achieved >90% knockdown at 24 hr and ~50% knockdown after 96 hr.
source: ASOs were nucleofected at a concentration of 2 µM, and we are able to achieve a >90% knockdown at 24 hr, and an ~50% knockdown was still achieved after 96 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Proliferation assays show a 50% reduction in proliferation at 4 days (96 hr) after ASO treatment.
source: Proliferation assays using manual cell counts and MTS assay show a 50% reduction in proliferation at 4 days (96 hr), similar to that achieved in our knockout clones, further supporting a role of PHAROH in cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Knockdown of PHAROH significantly inhibits clonogenic growth of HCC cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Colony formation assays demonstrated that knockdown of PHAROH significantly inhibits clonogenic growth of HCC cells in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: 810 differentially expressed genes were identified in PHAROH knockout cells by RNA-seq.
source: To investigate the global effect of PHAROH depletion, we performed poly(A)+RNA seq on control and knockout clones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B). We identified 810 differentially expressed genes, and GO term analysis revealed regulation of cell proliferation, locomotion, and cell motility as the highest enriched terms (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: GO term analysis of differentially expressed genes in PHAROH knockout cells revealed regulation of cell proliferation, locomotion, and cell motility as the highest enriched terms.
source: We identified 810 differentially expressed genes, and GO term analysis revealed regulation of cell proliferation, locomotion, and cell motility as the highest enriched terms (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: Promoter motif analysis of differentially expressed genes revealed enrichment of the Myc motif.
source: Interestingly, promoter motif analysis of differentially expressed genes revealed enrichment of the Myc motif in our dataset, suggesting a subset of the genes were under the transcriptional control of Myc (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: Myc expression changes were not detected in RNA-seq analysis of PHAROH knockout cells.
source: However, Myc expression changes were not detected in our RNA-seq analysis, nor was there any statistically significant change compared to sgRenilla controls when assayed by qRT-PCR (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B

claim: MYC protein levels were substantially decreased in all of the PHAROH knockout clones.
source: Strikingly, MYC protein levels were substantially decreased in all of the PHAROH knockout clones, as detected by western blot and immunofluorescence, suggesting that PHAROH regulates Myc post-transcriptionally (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E

claim: PHAROH regulates Myc post-transcriptionally.
source: Strikingly, MYC protein levels were substantially decreased in all of the PHAROH knockout clones, as detected by western blot and immunofluorescence, suggesting that PHAROH regulates Myc post-transcriptionally (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that MYC protein levels decrease without changes in mRNA levels

claim: Genes downstream of Myc identified through RNA-seq analysis were significantly downregulated in PHAROH knockout clones.
source: qRT-PCR of genes downstream of Myc that were identified through our analysis were also significantly downregulated in PHAROH knockout clones (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Four out of five biotinylated oligos antisense to PHAROH pulled down >80% of endogenous PHAROH.
source: To this end, we screened through five 20-mer 3′ biotinylated DNA oligos that tiled the length of PHAROH and found that four out of the five oligos pulled down >80% of endogenous PHAROH, while the pulldown of a control RNA, PPIB, remained low (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RAP-MS data shown in Figure 5A

claim: PHAROH can be eluted at a specific temperature, with maximum elution reached at 40°C.
source: For elution of PHAROH, we tested a range of temperatures and found that the elution efficiency reaches the maximum at 40°C, and thus we used this temperature for further experiments (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by temperature gradient elution data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Nucleolysin TIAR was identified as the top hit in RAP-MS analysis of PHAROH interacting proteins.
source: To identify proteins that bind to PHAROH, we analyzed two independent oligos that target PHAROH and two replicates of PPIB on a single 4-plex iTRAQ (isobaric tag for relative and absolute quantitation) mass spectrometry cassette and identified a total of 690 proteins. By plotting the log2 enrichment ratio of PHAROH hits divided by PPIB hits, quadrant I will contain proteins that both oligos against PHAROH recognize, and quadrant III will be enriched for proteins that bind specifically to PPIB. Quadrant III was enriched for keratins, elongation factors, and ribosomal proteins. Interestingly, the top hit in quadrant I is nucleolysin TIAR (TIAL-1), an RNA-binding protein that controls mRNA translation by binding to AU-rich elements in the 3′ UTR of mRNA (Figure 5C, Table 2; Mazan-Mamczarz et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by iTRAQ mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C and Table 2

claim: TIAR is an RNA-binding protein that controls mRNA translation by binding to AU-rich elements in the 3′ UTR of mRNA.
source: Interestingly, the top hit in quadrant I is nucleolysin TIAR (TIAL-1), an RNA-binding protein that controls mRNA translation by binding to AU-rich elements in the 3′ UTR of mRNA (Figure 5C, Table 2; Mazan-Mamczarz et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mazan-Mamczarz et al., 2006

claim: TIAR is present in <10% of all experiments queried on Crapome.org (31/411).
source: TIAR is present in <10% of all experiments queried on Crapome.org (31/411).
evidence: Supported by query of Crapome.org database

claim: Immunoblots for TIAR confirm that TIAR is specific to PHAROH pulldown oligos and is eluted at 40°C.
source: Immunoblots for TIAR confirm the mass spectrometry data in that TIAR is specific to PHAROH pulldown oligos and also is eluted at 40°C (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D

claim: RNase A treatment of the lysate largely abolished the TIAR-PHAROH interaction, indicating that the interaction is RNA mediated.
source: RNase A treatment of the lysate largely abolished the interaction, which indicates that the interaction is RNA mediated, and not the result of direct binding to the oligo (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by RNase A treatment data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Immunoprecipitation of TIAR enriches for PHAROH transcript when compared to IgG and PPIB control.
source: Immunoprecipitation of TIAR and subsequent extraction of interacting RNA shows enrichment for PHAROH when compared to PPIB and IgG control (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by IP-qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5F

claim: TIAR binding sites are enriched in the 5′ end of the PHAROH transcript of both isoforms.
source: A previous study on TIAR has mapped its RNA recognition motif (RRM) across the transcriptome (Meyer et al., 2018). Analysis of PHAROH's sequence reveals that TIAR binding sites are enriched in the 5′ end of the transcript of both isoforms (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Four out of seven TIAR binding sites in PHAROH consistently mapped to a hairpin that was conserved throughout all predicted structures.
source: The two strongest TIAR binding sequences (TTTT and ATTT/TTTA) were mapped onto 10 outputted predicted structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). Strikingly, four out of the seven binding sites consistently mapped to a hairpin that was conserved throughout all predicted structures.
evidence: Supported by RNA structure prediction analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Three of the strongest TIAR binding motifs localize to the stem of the PHAROH hairpin, while one secondary motif resides in a bulge.
source: Three of the strongest binding motifs localize to the stem of the hairpin, while one secondary motif resides in a bulge (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by structure analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: RNA EMSA of the 71-nt PHAROH hairpin with human recombinant TIAR shows three sequential shifts as TIAR concentration increases.
source: RNA electromobility shift assay (EMSA) of the hairpin and recombinant human TIAR showed that as TIAR concentration increases it binds to the PHAROH hairpin multiple times (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA data shown in Figure 6C

claim: TIAR has a preference to bind two and four times to the PHAROH hairpin, rather than once or three times.
source: TIAR has a preference to bind two and four times, rather than once or three times.
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA data shown in Figure 6C

claim: TIAR has an approximate dissociation constant of 2 nM for the PHAROH hairpin.
source: Densitometry quantification of the remaining free probe shows that TIAR has an approximate dissociation constant of 2 nM, consistent with the literature (Kim et al., 2011; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by densitometry analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Addition of an antibody against TIAR creates a supershift in RNA EMSA, showing that the interaction is specific.
source: Addition of an antibody against TIAR creates a supershift, showing that the interaction is specific, while addition of IgG does not.
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA data shown in Figure 6E

claim: The TIAR-PHAROH interaction can be abolished with addition of 20× unlabeled probe.
source: The interaction can be abolished with addition of 20× unlabeled probe as well (Figure 6E, left panel).
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA competition data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Mutation of the first TIAR binding site (m1) in the PHAROH hairpin slightly reduced specificity of TIAR to the hairpin, but changes the preference of TIAR binding to one and two units.
source: Mutation of the first binding site (m1) slightly reduced specificity of TIAR to the hairpin, but changes the preference of TIAR binding to one and two units (Figure 6E, right panel).
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA data with mutant hairpins shown in Figure 6E

claim: Mutation of two TIAR binding sites (m2) in the PHAROH hairpin greatly reduced TIAR association.
source: Mutation of m2 greatly reduced TIAR association, and only two bands are highly visible (Figure 6E, right panel).
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA data with mutant hairpins shown in Figure 6E

claim: Mutation of all four TIAR binding sites (m4) in the PHAROH hairpin showed minimal TIAR binding.
source: Mutation of all four binding sites (m4) showed minimal TIAR binding (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA data with mutant hairpins shown in Figure 6E

claim: TIAR binds directly to the 71-nt sequence on PHAROH, which can fold into a hairpin, and preferentially binds two or four times.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that TIAR binds directly to the 71-nt sequence on PHAROH, which can fold into a hairpin, and preferentially binds two or four times.
evidence: Based on inference from RNA EMSA data with wildtype and mutant hairpins

claim: TIAR has been shown to bind to the 3′ UTR of mRNAs containing AU-rich elements in order to inhibit their translation.
source: TIAR has been shown to bind to the 3′ UTR of mRNAs containing AU-rich elements in order to inhibit their translation (Mazan-Mamczarz et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mazan-Mamczarz et al., 2006

claim: TIAR binds to the 3′ UTR of Myc mRNA.
source: It has also been shown that TIAR binds to the 3′ UTR of Myc mRNA (Liao et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liao et al., 2007

claim: PHAROH serves to competitively sequester TIAR in order to allow for increased MYC translation.
source: Our data suggests that PHAROH serves to competitively sequester TIAR in order to allow for increased MYC translation.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental data including RAP-MS, RNA EMSA, and luciferase assays

claim: Knockout or knockdown of PHAROH will free additional TIAR molecules to bind to the 3′ UTR of Myc and inhibit its translation.
source: Thus, knockout or knockdown of PHAROH will free additional TIAR molecules to bind to the 3′ UTR of Myc and inhibit its translation.
evidence: Based on inference from the proposed mechanism

claim: PAR-CLIP reads show two distinct TIAR binding sequences on the human MYC mRNA, but only one sequence maps to the mouse genome.
source: Mapping PAR-CLIP reads from Meyer et al., 2018 shows two distinct binding sequences on the human MYC mRNA, but only one sequence maps to the mouse genome.
evidence: Supported by analysis of PAR-CLIP data from Meyer et al., 2018

claim: The 53-nt sequence in the Myc 3′ UTR has three distinct regions that are enriched in poly-uridines.
source: The stretch of 53-nt sequence has three distinct regions that are enriched in poly-uridines, but structural prediction largely places the sequences in a loop formation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by sequence and structure analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: RNA EMSA of the 53-nt Myc 3′ UTR and recombinant TIAR showed preference for a singular binding event.
source: RNA EMSA of the 53-nt 3′ UTR and recombinant TIAR showed preference for a singular binding event, and three events are only seen when the binding reaction is saturated by TIAR (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA data shown in Figure 7A

claim: ASO-mediated knockdown of PHAROH shows reduction of MYC protein similar to the knockouts, but no change in mRNA levels, or TIAR protein levels.
source: ASO-mediated knockdown of PHAROH shows reduction of MYC protein similar to the knockouts, but no change in mRNA levels, or TIAR protein levels (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: Myc is only threefold more expressed than PHAROH in HCC cell lines.
source: While mRNAs are generally much more highly expressed than lncRNAs, Myc is only threefold more expressed than PHAROH in HCC cell lines (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The wildtype PHAROH hairpin can compete with Myc 3′ UTR for TIAR binding very effectively at nearly all tested ratios, with near complete competition at 10:1 ratio.
source: Next, we tested this hypothesis in vitro by allowing TIAR to bind to the 53-nt Myc 3′ UTR and titrating increasing amounts of PHAROH or the mutant PHAROH transcript. The wildtype PHAROH hairpin can be seen to compete with Myc very effectively at nearly all tested ratios, with near complete competition at 10:1 ratio (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA competition data shown in Figure 7C

claim: The fully mutant PHAROH was not able to compete with Myc 3′ UTR for TIAR binding nearly as effectively as wildtype PHAROH.
source: However, the fully mutant PHAROH was not able to compete with Myc nearly as effectively and was only seen to be slightly effective at the 10:1 ratio (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by RNA EMSA competition data shown in Figure 7C

claim: PHAROH has the capability to successfully compete with the Myc 3′ UTR binding site in a sequence-dependent manner.
source: This data suggests that the PHAROH has the capability to successfully compete with the Myc 3′ UTR binding site in a sequence-dependent manner.
evidence: Based on inference from RNA EMSA competition data

claim: Addition of PHAROH increases luciferase signal by ~50% in a dose-dependent manner in a dual luciferase reporter construct with the full-length Myc 3′ UTR.
source: In addition, we cloned the full-length Myc 3′ UTR into a dual luciferase reporter construct in order to test our hypothesis in cells. We found that addition of PHAROH does indeed increase the luciferase signal by ~50% in a dose-dependent manner while the mutant PHAROH did not (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D

claim: Mutant PHAROH did not increase luciferase signal in the dual luciferase reporter construct with the full-length Myc 3′ UTR.
source: We found that addition of PHAROH does indeed increase the luciferase signal by ~50% in a dose-dependent manner while the mutant PHAROH did not (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D

claim: Overexpression of PHAROH increases MYC protein levels compared to GFP transfection.
source: Given that the knockdown or knockout of PHAROH reduces MYC levels due to the release of TIAR, we asked whether MYC protein levels would change in the context of PHAROH overexpression. Compared to GFP transfection, overexpression of PHAROH increases MYC protein levels; however, overexpression of mutant PHAROH did not change the protein levels of MYC (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7E

claim: Overexpression of mutant PHAROH did not change the protein levels of MYC.
source: Compared to GFP transfection, overexpression of PHAROH increases MYC protein levels; however, overexpression of mutant PHAROH did not change the protein levels of MYC (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7E

claim: Modulation of PHAROH or TIAR levels did not have an effect on Myc mRNA levels.
source: Modulation of PHAROH or TIAR levels did not have an effect on Myc mRNA levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E

claim: MYC is well known to be associated with HCC and is amplified in nearly 50% of HCC tumors.
source: Modulation of PHAROH levels reveals that it is positively correlated with MYC protein level, which is well known to be associated with HCC and is amplified in nearly 50% of HCC tumors (Peng et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peng et al., 1993

claim: MYC has been characterized as a critical player in liver regeneration.
source: In addition, MYC has been characterized as a critical player in liver regeneration (Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2017

claim: TIAR is known for its role in stress granules.
source: While TIAR is an RNA-binding protein that is known for its role in stress granules (Kedersha et al., 1999), we do not detect stress granule formation in our HCC cell lines as assayed by immunofluorescence for TIAR (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kedersha et al., 1999

claim: Stress granule formation was not detected in HCC cell lines as assayed by immunofluorescence for TIAR.
source: While TIAR is an RNA-binding protein that is known for its role in stress granules (Kedersha et al., 1999), we do not detect stress granule formation in our HCC cell lines as assayed by immunofluorescence for TIAR (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F

claim: The role of PHAROH-TIAR lies outside the context of stress granule function.
source: As such, the role of PHAROH-TIAR lies outside the context of stress granule function.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that stress granules are not detected in HCC cell lines

claim: Overexpression of TIAR is a negative prognostic marker for HCC survival.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of TIAR is a negative prognostic marker for HCC survival (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G; Uhlen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and citation to Uhlen et al., 2017

claim: TIAR may be upregulated in HCC in an attempt to curb MYC expression.
source: As the primary mutation of HCC is commonly amplification of MYC, it is possible that TIAR is upregulated in an attempt to curb MYC expression.
evidence: Based on speculation from the observation that TIAR overexpression is a negative prognostic marker

claim: The PHAROH-TIAR interaction predominantly occurs at a 71-nt hairpin at the 5′ end of PHAROH.
source: Our analysis maps the PHAROH-TIAR interaction to predominantly occur at a 71-nt hairpin at the 5′ end of PHAROH.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and RNA EMSA data

claim: The PHAROH hairpin is commonly expressed in both isoforms of PHAROH.
source: While PHAROH has two main isoforms that are selectively expressed in ESCs and HCC, the hairpin is commonly expressed in both isoforms.
evidence: Supported by RACE and RNA-seq data

claim: TIAR has a dissociation constant of ~1 nM for U-rich sequences and ~14 µM for AU-rich sequences.
source: Kinetic and affinity studies have found that TIAR has a dissociation constant of ~1 nM for U-rich sequences and ~14 µM for AU-rich sequences (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2011

claim: TIAR binds efficiently to uridylate residues of 3–11 length.
source: It has been reported that TIAR binds efficiently to uridylate residues of 3–11 length, yet PAR-CLIP data only reveals two binding events in the human MYC transcript (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2011

claim: The average gap between TIAR binding sites in the Myc 3′ UTR fragment is 2 nt, while it is 10 nt in the PHAROH hairpin.
source: The average gap between binding sites in the Myc fragment is 2 nt, while it is 10 nt in the PHAROH hairpin, which allows more flexibility in spacing between each bound protein.
evidence: Based on analysis of sequence data

claim: The 10 nt gap between TIAR binding sites in the PHAROH hairpin allows more flexibility in spacing between each bound protein.
source: The average gap between binding sites in the Myc fragment is 2 nt, while it is 10 nt in the PHAROH hairpin, which allows more flexibility in spacing between each bound protein.
evidence: Based on inference from sequence analysis

claim: TIAR's RRM2 mainly mediates ssRNA polyU-binding.
source: TIAR contains three RRMs, which typically recognizes single-stranded RNA. Therefore, binding of TIAR to the 71-nt sequence of PHAROH would require unwinding of the potential hairpin, which is energetically unfavorable. It is also known that TIAR's RRM2 mainly mediates ssRNA polyU-binding, but its dsRNA binding capabilities have not been explored (Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013

claim: TIAR was initially studied in immune cells and was shown to predominantly translationally repress Tnf-α through binding of the AU-rich sequence in the 3′ UTR.
source: This seems to be cell type specific as TIAR was initially studied in immune cells and was shown to predominantly translationally repress Tnf-α through binding of the AU-rich sequence in the 3′ UTR (Piecyk et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piecyk et al., 2000

claim: Tnf-α is not expressed in the HCC cell lines used in this study.
source: In our cell lines, Tnf-α is not expressed.
evidence: Based on observation in the experimental system

claim: lncRNA MT1JP functions as a tumor suppressor and has the capability to bind to TIAR, which suppresses the translation of p53.
source: Another recent study had shown that lncRNA MT1JP functions as a tumor suppressor and had the capability to bind to TIAR, which suppresses the translation of p53 (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016

claim: MT1JP is largely cytoplasmic, while TIAR in the HCC context is mainly nuclear.
source: However, MT1JP is largely cytoplasmic, while TIAR in our context is mainly nuclear.
evidence: Based on comparison with published data and observations in this study

claim: One of the main targets of TIAR in HCC cell lines is Myc, as supported by statistically significant promoter enrichment of the downstream targets.
source: Thus, while TIAR may bind additional mRNAs or lncRNAs, it seems that one of the main targets in HCC cell lines is Myc, as supported by statistically significant promoter enrichment of the downstream targets.
evidence: Based on inference from motif analysis and experimental data

claim: LINC00862 is the possible human ortholog of PHAROH based on synteny and upregulation in human HCC samples.
source: In summary, we have identified a lncRNA, PHAROH, that is enriched in ESCs and dysregulated in HCC, and found that it acts to sequester TIAR through a hairpin structure in order to regulate MYC translation. Additionally, based on synteny and upregulation in human HCC samples, we identified LINC00862 as the possible human ortholog of PHAROH (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on synteny analysis and expression data in human samples

claim: Future studies will reveal the therapeutic potential of targeting PHAROH to impact liver development/regeneration and HCC.
source: Future studies will reveal the therapeutic potential of targeting PHAROH to impact liver development/regeneration and HCC.
evidence: Speculative statement about future research directions
